newsitem.title: USA: Nova Scotia says Sable natgas project on schedule.
newsitem.headline: Nova Scotia says Sable natgas project on schedule.

text.p: The premier of Nova Scotia, where a huge offshore natural gas project called Sable is being developed by private companies, said Wednesday consumers should start getting the benefits in 1999.

"The project is on schedule. We anticipate regulatory and govermental approvals will be in place this fall," John Savage, the premier of Nova Scotia, said at the Annual Conference of the New England Governors and Eastern Canadian Premiers.
Noting a number of construction projects already had begun although the approval process was not yet finished, he added: "We're confident Sable gas will be available to consumers at the end of 1999."

He cited estimates that showed there are approximately three trillion cubic feet of natural gas at Sable, which will help supply New England states with natural gas. Savage also sought to soothe local concerns about how much of the energy Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will get.
"There is no question that we will have access to the gas," he said.

A controversy over where the project's pipeline network should be built showed no sign of letting up, as the premier of Quebec, Lucien Bouchard, reminded the gathering that an alternative plan he supports would be completely filed with Canada regulators by the summer.

"By August, the full project could be exposed to the Board, to allow it to make an assessment," he said, explaining this route would have to be judged on his merits, just like the competing pipeline proposed by Maritimes & Northeast, whose partners include Westcoast Energy Inc, PanEnergy Corp and Mobil Corp unit Mobil Canada. That proposal already is being considered by Canada's federal regulators.

The Maritimes & Northeast pipeline would send the gas to New England by traveling from Nova Scotia to New Brunswick and Maine, but bypass Quebec. In contrast, the competing project Bouchard backs, put forward by TransCanada PipeLines Ltd and Gaz Matropolitain would send the natgas through Quebec.

Savage reacted to Bouchard's comments by again stressing that a timely decision by Canada's regulators in selecting a pipeline route was needed. "The only point I would raise is that the window of opportunity is created by changing markets. That is why the time element that everybody refers to is so important."

The premier of New Brunswick did not take a stand on which pipeline route he supported, noting both of the projects proposed would go through his province. "We have yearned for natural gas for a long, long time," said Frank McKenna, noting that the province suddenly has gone from having no choices to two, both of which had to be carefully weighed to see which offered the province the most benefit.

Saying the situation before him was a bit like a fight in an ice-cream store over flavors, McKenna added: "For us, having gas is a very important thing and I don't like people to lose sight of that fact." He declined to comment on when a decision might be forthcoming.

Another big energy project in Canada also was on track as the Jeanne D'Arc basin in Newfoundland, which has 1.6 billion barrels of proven reserves, will start producing oil this year, according to Brian Tobin, the premier of Newfoundland and Labrador. He added that estimates showed the Hibernia project has 4.5 trillion cubic feet of natural gas proven reserves, with another 4.5 off the coast of Labrador.

Asked about the potential for linking the Jeanne D'Arc development to the Sable project's network of pipelines, Nova Scotia's premier noted that while the two groups share some of the same partners, Sable was being developed privately.
"The opportunity to utilize the existing infrastructure is fundamentally an issue that will be up to the private sector and our government will not be interfering in any way."
Later, he added, "We will encourage that, sure."

New England's thirst for Canada's new supplies of natural gas and hydroelectric power was highlighted by some of the energy analysts and New England governors, who noted the region pays some of the highest rates in the nation. The New England states now import over 90 percent of their energy, according to an economist who spoke at the conference.

Vito Stagliano, an analyst with Energy Security Analysis said: "Historically energy poor New England is suddenly finding itself at the center of one of the most competitive markets in the United States."

Pointing to several of the big energy projects in the Eastern Canada provinces whose potential was outlined at the conference, Maine's Gov Angus King concluded: "It makes us Texas without the rattle-snakes."
